coverage: Nine stories · Java4Shell, tainted web scripts, light chips, Gemini privacy, YouTube TV views, Waymo, San Diego cameras, Voyager 1, glowing robot

cards.headline: AI-assisted researchers find critical flaw in Java's Base64 decoder
cards.summary: Calif Research disclosed Java4Shell, a memory-corruption bug in OpenJDK, the free software that runs Java programs. It sits in a sped-up Base64 decoder (Base64 turns binary data into plain text) used only on some x86 processors, the kind in many PCs and servers. Bad input can overwrite nearby memory and, in some apps, let an attacker take control. Calif says one researcher found it in about an hour with OpenAI's Codex. Oracle and OpenJDK released fixes Tuesday.
cards.whyItMatters: Java runs inside banking, airline and login systems, so one bug can affect many apps at once. No attacks using it had been reported yet, which is why quick updates matter.

csp.connection: A program that writes past the end of its memory buffer can corrupt other data; checking lengths and boundaries prevents this.

cards.headline: Tampered website code put malware on 178 major sites
cards.summary: Optimizely supplies JavaScript that many websites load to test and personalize pages. Researchers at ReportURI say attackers slipped malicious code into those scripts, which then ran on at least 178 sites, including CNN, Zoom, the BBC and Salesforce. The code swapped cryptocurrency wallet addresses, copied card numbers typed into some forms and tried to infect older iPhones. How attackers got in is still unknown; Optimizely had not responded.
cards.whyItMatters: When a site loads code from another company, that code runs with the site's full trust. Keeping your phone updated blocks many attacks that target old software.

csp.connection: Web pages often combine code from many servers, so one compromised supplier can affect every site that depends on it.

cards.headline: Europe bets €400 million on chips that compute with light
cards.summary: Most chips move electrons through billions of tiny transistors. Photonic chips process data with light instead, which supporters say can be faster, use less energy and run cooler. The European Union has committed €400 million to a project called PIX Europe, and the Dutch research institute TNO is building a factory in Eindhoven to make larger photonic chip wafers. It is due to fully open in 2030.
cards.whyItMatters: AI data centers need ever more power, so more efficient chips could cut energy use. A TNO leader says photonics is where electronic chips were 40 to 50 years ago.

csp.connection: Hardware sets the limits on how fast and efficiently a computer can process data, and new designs can shift those limits.

cards.headline: Gemini users can now keep chat history without training Google's AI
cards.summary: Before, the only way to stop Google from using your Gemini chats to train its AI was to turn off your chat history. A new setting, rolling out globally over several weeks, separates the two, though you must find the toggle and switch training off yourself. It only affects future chats. Separately, U.S. users on paid plans are getting a way to view and edit the memory summary Gemini builds about them.
cards.whyItMatters: Many people pass personal details to chatbots without thinking about where they go. Knowing these settings lets you decide what you share, though Google may still keep data for other uses.

csp.connection: Data you give an app can be stored and reused in ways you may not expect, so default settings shape what happens to your information.

cards.headline: YouTube will estimate extra viewers when videos play on a TV
cards.summary: YouTube says it has been undercounting views when several people watch together on a TV. It will add estimated co-views to public view counts and watch time for TV viewing only. YouTube says it won't use cameras or microphones; a statistical model based on patterns like demographics and viewing times will make the estimate. The change won't apply to old views and won't affect how much money creators earn.
cards.whyItMatters: View counts influence what creators make and what brands sponsor. These numbers will now be partly estimates, and YouTube hasn't shared full details of its model.

csp.connection: Statistical models can estimate things that aren't measured directly, but their results are only as good as their assumptions.

cards.headline: Waymo pauses robotaxi freeway rides after California ban
cards.summary: California's Department of Motor Vehicles barred Waymo's driverless cars from state freeways on November 11, calling them an imminent hazard to public safety. It cited repeated cases of the cars entering active construction zones, including three that drove into one on U.S. 101. No injuries or collisions were reported. Waymo has now paused freeway rides in all its U.S. cities but still operates on city streets.
cards.whyItMatters: Self-driving software must handle rare, messy situations like work zones, not just ordinary roads. The ban stays until Waymo shows regulators it has fixed the problem.

csp.connection: Software that makes decisions in the physical world needs testing on unusual cases, because errors can affect public safety.

cards.headline: San Diego votes to switch off license plate cameras
cards.summary: San Diego's city council voted to end contracts with Flock, which makes automatic license plate readers (cameras whose software records passing plates), and with a smart streetlight company whose lights worked with them. More than 500 cameras will go dark. Police told the council the cameras helped recover 689 stolen vehicles, and Flock warned crimes may take longer to solve. Privacy advocates had argued the system tracked residents' movements.
cards.whyItMatters: Cities must weigh crime-solving tools against how much location data they collect about everyone. San Diego is one of the largest cities to end a Flock contract.

csp.connection: Automated data collection can serve public safety while also raising privacy concerns about tracking ordinary people.

cards.headline: Voyager 1 is now one light-day from Earth
cards.summary: Launched in 1977, NASA's Voyager 1 crossed a milestone Wednesday: it is now about 16.1 billion miles away, the distance light travels in 24 hours. It is the farthest human-made object and still sends data on particles and magnetic fields. Radio signals now take a full day to reach it. Separately, a historian found that the Golden Record it carries repeats its playback instructions inside its cover as a backup.
cards.whyItMatters: Engineers must plan every command knowing the reply arrives two days later. Repeating key instructions in case one copy wears away is the same backup idea used in computer systems.

csp.connection: Distance adds latency, the delay before data arrives, and redundant copies help information survive if one copy fails.

cards.headline: Soft robot glows green wherever its body stretches
cards.summary: Researchers at South Korea's DGIST built a small four-limbed soft robot covered in a woven mesh of flexible tubes. The tubes are filled with zinc sulfide particles mixed into a stretchy polymer, which glows green where the material is stretched, with no batteries or electronics. The fibers kept glowing after more than 1,000 stretches. The study appears in the journal Small Structures.
cards.whyItMatters: Soft robots bend in ways that are hard to monitor with stiff sensors. A body that lights up where it strains could help engineers spot problems, and may lead to wearable medical devices.

csp.connection: Robots rely on sensors to report their own state, and new materials can turn a robot's body into a sensor.
